title: Roman doctors preface object- vs subject-certainty; the question concerns the latter
source_text: I. Ut suam hac de re sententiam exponunt Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, multas certitudinis distinctiones praemittunt; ut videre est apud Bellarminum de Justificatione, lib. 3. cap. 2. Primo enim ipsis una est certitudo objecti, id est, rei cognitae, vel creditae; altera vero subjecti, id est, hominis cognoscentis, vel credentis. Prior certitudo est immutabilitas rei, quae revera aliter se habere non potest, quam creditur, vel cognoscitur. Qua ratione dicimus certum esse Deum esse bonum, peccatum esse malum. Posterior certitudo est firmitas quaedam assensus nostri ad rem quae credenda, vel cognoscenda proponitur. De qua certitudine loquimur, quum dicimus hac de re certus sum, hoc mihi compertum est; id est, ita firmiter adhaereo huic sententiae, ut prorsus de illius veritate non dubitem. Ad praesentem autem quaestionem pertinet certitudo non prioris, sed posterioris generis.
pass_a_gloss: As the doctors of the Roman Church set out their opinion on this matter, they preface many distinctions of certainty; as may be seen in Bellarmine On Justification, book 3, chapter 2. For first they have one certainty of the object, that is, of the thing known or believed; and another of the subject, that is, of the knowing or believing person. The former certainty is the immutability of the thing, which in reality cannot be otherwise than it is believed or known. In that sense we say it is certain that God is good and that sin is evil. The latter certainty is a certain firmness of our assent to the thing proposed to be believed or known. Of this certainty we speak when we say, concerning this matter I am certain, this is ascertained to me; that is, I so firmly adhere to this judgment that I do not doubt at all of its truth. But to the present question belongs certainty not of the former but of the latter kind.
pass_b_english: Roman doctors begin with Bellarmine’s distinction between certainty of the object and of the believing subject.
Object-certainty is the thing’s immutability; subject-certainty is firm assent without doubt—and that latter sense is the one at issue here.
